alert_pattern: [FIRING:1] <cluster> : KubePersistentVolumeFillingUp - PVC <name> in <cluster> is only N% free
environment: any k8s cluster (seen on transcode scratch storage)
diagnosis_steps: Extract PVC name and namespace from alert (alert body includes 'PVC <name> filling up in <cluster>' and % free)
Confirm current usage on the storage dashboard; post the panel screenshot showing % free
Check whether the writer is a transcode/scratch workload - these fill during big jobs and MAY self-recover when the job completes
Check the runbook link embedded in the alert (Runbook: KubePersistentVolumeFillingUp - Resizing PVCs)
resolution_steps: Resize the PVC upward (observed: +50GB on a volume at ~8% free), per the resizing-PVCs runbook
Verify free space recovers (observed: 8% -> 39% free after adding 50GB)
Post the after screenshot in thread; resolved
gotchas: PVCs only grow, never shrink - size increases are permanent cost
Ack the VictorOps incident early so it doesn't escalate while you work
escalation: App owner if the same PVC needs resizing repeatedly (indicates a leak/retention problem, not capacity)

alert_pattern: [FIRING:N] <cluster> : KubePodsNotReady (often N in the tens; engine pods)
environment: any aiWARE k8s cluster; usually engine pods
diagnosis_steps: START FROM THE CARD, not from kubectl: there is one sub-alert PER POD, each with a `pod` label, and sometimes `owner_kind` (observed `DaemonSet` on #121443). That list is what the next step would otherwise have to rebuild, and the SHARED `eng-<8hex>--` prefix across those pod names is the 'one root cause, not N problems' finding - available before any cluster call. Then use kubectl to get what the card cannot carry: current state, exit codes and logs. Remember the card's `namespace` label is the ALERT's (`central-monitoring`), never the pod's (`aiware`).
List not-ready pods and bucket by state: kubectl get pods -n aiware | grep -vE 'Running|Completed' - states seen: ImagePullBackOff, CrashLoopBackOff, Error, Pending/Init

ImagePullBackOff: verify the image tag actually exists in the registry (docker manifest inspect <image>); also check engine BUILD state - builds not in 'Deployed' state have caused pulls of unavailable images
Pending with FailedScheduling: read the event - node taints observed (ToBeDeletedByClusterAutoscaler, uninitialized, network-unavailable) usually mean node churn in progress
Error/CrashLoop: grep pod logs for the failure signature: panic|fatal|context deadline|Throttl|OOM|connection refused

Engine pods in `Error` (not CrashLoop): grep every one of them for the SAME first failure line before concluding anything - `for p in $(kubectl get pods -n aiware --no-headers | awk '$1 ~ /^eng-<prefix>--/ && $3=="Error"{print $1}'); do kubectl logs $p -n aiware | grep -m1 -E 'Failed to connect|terminated due to'; done`. 2026-09-11 on aiw-prod1001: all 8 Error pods showed `SSConnCache.GetConn Failed to connect to edge-storage-server-5...:50051, err=context deadline exceeded` within a 3-minute window, which is what proved one root cause rather than eight.

When the log names a dependency, check that dependency's CURRENT state before proposing anything: `kubectl get sts,pods -n aiware -o wide | grep edge-storage-server`. It was 9/9 Running and healthy by the time the alert was investigated - the outage had already passed.
Common crash signature: engine toolkit 'Failed to start subprocess [/opt/runner] err=context deadline exceeded' = engine couldn't reach the edge controller at startup
Check node health for the affected pods (kubectl describe node - pressure conditions, Ready history)
Check whether an ongoing change (cluster upgrade, controller rollout, load test) explains it - link the change thread
resolution_steps: Dependency already recovered: the dead pods do NOT clear themselves. Confirm new engine pods are running, then bulk-delete the stale `Error` pods (observed 2026-09-11: 8 pods, 10h old, deleted after edge-storage-server-5 was verified healthy).
Bulk-delete pods stuck in Error so the controller recreates them (observed 3500+ Error pods deleted at once)
If new pods immediately re-enter Error with the same log signature, deleting is futile - the dependency (edge controller / registry) is the problem; fix that first
For engine builds not Deployed: deploy the builds, pods recover
For autoscaler taint churn: usually self-heals as nodes finish cycling; monitor
Confirm backlogs drain after pods recover; resolved
gotchas: FIRING count is inflated - 50 crashlooping pods is usually ONE root cause (one engine build, one dependency, one node event)
If controller pods were rolled after the incident window, the relevant logs are gone - note it and move on rather than guessing
Deleting Error pods without checking the crash signature just burns scheduler cycles when the root cause persists
A pod's age is evidence: 10h-old `Error` pods next to healthy new ones mean the fault is OVER and only the corpses remain. Report it as a past incident with a cleanup, not as an ongoing outage.
escalation: Engine/platform team when the crash is inside engine code or builds need redeployment
example_commands: kubectl get pods -n aiware --no-headers | grep eng | awk '{count[$3]++} END {for (s in count) print s, count[s]}'

known_root_causes.cause: Engine pods could not reach one edge-storage-server replica at startup and terminated. All 8 failing pods hit the same replica (-5) between 15:33 and 15:35 UTC on 2026-09-10.
known_root_causes.status: self-recovered - the StatefulSet was 9/9 Running when investigated; the stale Error pods were deleted by hand

alert_payload.description: Pod has been in a non-ready state for more than 15 minutes.
labels: namespace (always central-monitoring - the ALERT's namespace, NOT the pod's)
owner_kind (ONLY when the pod has a controller - observed 'DaemonSet' on #121443, absent on the bare engine pods of #121450/#121465)
alert_payload.use_it_for: Every failing pod name is in the card, one sub-alert each - that is the list list_unhealthy_pods would otherwise have to rebuild. The shared `eng-<8hex>--` prefix across them is the engine, and finding one shared prefix across 230 sub-alerts IS the 'one root cause, not N problems' finding.
alert_payload.trap: `namespace: central-monitoring` is where the alert rule lives, not where the pod runs (the pods are in `aiware`). Using it as the kubectl namespace returns nothing. Also: the Started stamp can be over a day before the card (#121465 started 2026-09-10 07:59 UTC, resolved 2026-09-11 08:00 UTC) - these are long-lived, so check the age before calling it new.
alert_payload._shared: The parser now hands you these already split out, under 'sub-alerts parsed from state_message', with the FIRING ones listed first. Read them instead of re-reading the raw card. The block is only present while the incident is live — once VictorOps closes it the whole thing is replaced by 'Automatically resolved', and a block can be marked truncated, which means its missing fields are UNKNOWN rather than empty.
alert_payload.labels_vary: THE LABEL SET IS NOT FIXED, not even between sub-alerts of the SAME alert. Read the labels each block actually carries; never assume a label is there and never report one as absent from memory. `owner_kind` is the example that matters here: when it is present it answers the blast-radius question directly - `owner_kind: DaemonSet` is the signal to lead with the node spread, per the DaemonSet rule in the pod format - and when it is absent the pod is unowned and deleting it will NOT bring it back.

resolution_time_note: No single typical duration, and the old '60' was wrong. Measured from the cards' own Started/Resolved stamps: `9` minutes for a DaemonSet pod that self-recovered (#121443) and `1441` minutes - a full day - for an engine pod on #121465 that sat not-ready from 2026-09-10 07:59 UTC to 2026-09-11 08:00 UTC. Check the Started stamp before calling one of these new; a day-old pod is a cleanup, not an outage. (Found 2026-09-12 by py/scripts/inventory_gaps.py as RESOLUTION TIME DRIFT.)

alert_pattern: [FIRING:N] <cluster> : NodeHighCPUUsage - Node <node>.ec2.internal [<server_type>, <zone>] in cluster <cluster> has CPU above 90% for 15+ minutes. VALUE = <pct>
environment: aiw-prod1001 and aiw-prd5001 observed; labels carry env, node, instance (<ip>:9100), server_type, zone
resolution_time_note: Measured from the alert's own Started/Resolved stamps across 7 sub-alerts on 2026-09-11: 1, 1, 12, 12, 12, 12 and 15 minutes. It auto-resolves without anyone touching the node - the NOC posts the WHY, not a fix.
diagnosis_steps: The alert names the node in its labels (`node`, and `instance` as <ip>:9100). That is the only thing it names - which pod is burning the CPU is not in the alert.

Rank the nodes: `kubectl top nodes --sort-by=cpu`. Confirms the alerting node is really at the top and shows whether it is one node or several (2026-09-10 on aiw-prd5001: three nodes at 98-99% simultaneously).
Find what is running there: `kubectl top pods -n aiware --sort-by=cpu` filtered to that node. In every observed case the answer was engine pods named `eng-<engineId prefix>--<taskId>`.

Turn the pod-name prefix into an engine: the 8 hex chars after `eng-` are the head of the engine ID. 2026-09-10: `eng-90fcaf22--*` = `90fcaf22-048c-4a2a-83b0-717057184df1` = 'Pangeanic Translation (2022) - Traditional Chinese to English', pulling over 4,000 mCPU per pod.
Say how much work is in flight - the count of RUNNING/PENDING tasks for that engine is the number that explains the CPU (2026-09-11: '179 tasks in a running state').
Screenshot the pod CPU view and the task view; those two pictures plus the node name are the whole thread.
resolution_steps: Report the driving engine, its pod CPU and its running/pending task count, and stop. Every observed occurrence auto-resolved as the tasks finished.
Escalate only if the same engine pins the same node repeatedly, or if the node is NOT `server_type: engine_segregated` - engine load on a non-engine node is the abnormal case.
gotchas: `server_type: engine_segregated` means the node exists to run engine workload. Near-100% CPU there is saturation by design, not a fault - do not report it as a failure.
VALUE in the description is the exact CPU percent at evaluation time (observed 90.19 to 99.99) - quote it rather than re-deriving it.

Several sub-alerts arrive under one incident ([FIRING:9] on incident #121477) and they are usually different nodes driven by the SAME engine - find the shared engine, do not report N separate problems.
It resolves itself in about 12 minutes, so by the time the investigation runs the node may already be normal. Say the window it covered; a recovered node is a finding, not a failed investigation.
The node is named `ip-10-0-x-y.ec2.internal` while `instance` is `10.0.x.y:9100` - the same machine in two spellings.
escalation: Engine team only when one engine repeatedly saturates nodes; otherwise no escalation - the NOC posts the driving engine and the task count.
example_commands: kubectl get pods -n aiware -o wide --no-headers | awk '$8=="<node>"' | grep '^eng-'
_source: Built 2026-09-11 from two real #comms-noc threads plus the Started/Resolved stamps of 7 sub-alerts in #alerts-devops.

alert_payload._verified: incident #121477, 2026-09-11, read from the real card
alert_payload.summary: High CPU: <server_type> node in <env> (<zone>) - names the ROLE and the zone, not the node.
alert_payload.description: Node <node>.ec2.internal [<server_type>, <zone>] in cluster <env> has CPU above 90% for 15+ minutes. VALUE = <exact percent>. The node AND the exact percent are both here - quote VALUE rather than re-deriving the number from a graph.
alert_payload.use_it_for: `node` is the kubectl target and `instance` is the same machine as Prometheus knows it - no lookup needed. `server_type: engine_segregated` is what tells you saturation is by design. One card carries one sub-alert PER NODE, so the firing count is a node count.
alert_payload.trap: VictorOps renders RESOLVED sub-alerts FIRST. The node in the first block is often the one that already recovered; investigate a FIRING one. label_hints already prefers firing for this reason.

alertname: ArgoCD App Unhealthy / ArgoCD AutoSync Disabled
alert_pattern: [FIRING:N]  : ArgoCD App Unhealthy  |  [FIRING:N]  : ArgoCD AutoSync Disabled (the environment segment is EMPTY on both - argocd-prod is in the labels, not the title)
environment: argocd-prod (argocd5.ops.veritone.com); the App's own dest_namespace/dest_server say which cluster it targets
resolution_time_note: Not self-resolving. The one fully diagnosed occurrence needed a human ownership decision and was still open when the thread ended.
diagnosis_steps: Name the Application. AutoSync Disabled puts it in the summary ('ArgoCD auto-sync disabled for aiware-stgqrf') with the App URL in the description; App Unhealthy needs the ArgoCD UI to identify it (observed: `gitops-xk5-bootstrap` in Degraded state).
Open the App in ArgoCD and read WHICH resources are degraded - the App-level status is a rollup and says nothing on its own.
For a Degraded App, the degraded child resources are the finding (observed: 2 SealedSecret objects reporting `failed update`).
For AutoSync Disabled, the labels carry `autosync_enabled: false`, `health_status`, `dest_namespace` and `dest_server` - report those and whether anyone announced disabling it deliberately.
Check #comms-noc and the change channels for a deploy or ITSM window that explains a deliberately disabled auto-sync before treating it as a fault.
resolution_steps: SealedSecret ownership conflict: a human decides who should own the Secret. The sealed-secrets controller will never overwrite a Secret it does not own, so it refuses, reports `failed update`, and stays Degraded until that decision is made.
Re-syncing is not a fix for that case and must not be proposed - the controller will refuse again.
Auto-sync disabled on purpose for a deploy or migration: report the owning change and leave it.
gotchas: Degraded does NOT mean down. In the observed SealedSecret case both clusters kept working - the old Secret was present and valid. It is an ownership conflict, not an outage, and the thread must say so or it reads as a production incident.
Auto-sync will never clear this by itself, and repeated re-syncs will not either - stating that saves the next person from trying.
The alert title's environment segment is empty on both variants, so the usual '<env> : <alertname>' split yields nothing - take the environment from the labels.
escalation: The team that owns the Application and, for a SealedSecret conflict, whoever owns the conflicting Secret - that ownership call is the actual blocker.
_source: Built 2026-09-11 from the #comms-noc thread on incident #121427 and the #alerts-devops payload of incident #121475.

alert_payload.description: App <app> (project <project>, namespace <ns>) has had autosync_enabled=false for over 10 minutes. App: <the argocd5.ops.veritone.com URL>. The App URL is in the payload - cite it rather than constructing one.
alert_payload.use_it_for: `health_status` says whether the App is Healthy while auto-sync is off - Healthy + autosync-disabled is a config state, not an outage. `dest_server`/`dest_namespace` name the cluster and namespace the App targets, which is what makes the blast radius concrete.
alert_payload.trap: `environment: argocd-prod` is the ArgoCD instance, not the target env - `dest_server` is the target.
